---
title: "Student Lecture"
---

Once this semester you lead the class for 20 minutes, on something the course
never covers.

## Rules

- 15 to 20 minutes, once in the semester.
- Alone, or in a team of up to three.
- 10 points of your final grade. Every member of a team gets the same score.
- The class has to **do** something while you are up there. A talk on its own does not pass.
- Choose one topic from the pools below and one slot from the table. One topic per team, one slot per team.
- Put your names, your topic and your slot on the [sign-up sheet]({{< var signup.student_lecture >}}). First team on a row takes it.
- Bring me a one page plan at office hours, a week before your date.
- You may propose your own topic instead. Check that it appears nowhere in the course, and say what the class will do.

## What "do something" means

Good:

- everyone fills in a worksheet
- everyone works a small example by hand
- everyone writes down a guess before you reveal the answer
- everyone plays a short game
- you write code live and the class decides what to try next

Not enough:

- "any questions?"
- a poll that changes nothing
- a demo the class watches
- a quiz at the end

The self-check: if the class had stayed home, would your 20 minutes look the
same? If so, the activity is decoration.

## Topic pools

Twenty-six areas, none of them covered elsewhere in the course. Each is broader
than a single lecture, so you choose the angle. The reference is one place to
start reading.

### Kinds of network

- **SL-01 Bipartite networks.** Two types of node, and what a projection onto one type does. *Start:* Newman, *Networks*.
- **SL-02 Signed networks.** Links that mean friend or foe, and structural balance. *Start:* Cartwright and Harary, Psychological Review 1956.
- **SL-03 Higher-order networks.** Hypergraphs and simplicial complexes, where a single interaction joins more than two nodes. *Start:* Battiston et al., Physics Reports 2020.
- **SL-04 Multilayer and interdependent networks.** Several networks on the same nodes, and networks that depend on each other. *Start:* Kivela et al., Journal of Complex Networks 2014. Buldyrev et al., Nature 2010.

### Dynamics on networks

The structure stays fixed.

- **SL-05 Epidemic models.** SIR and SIS on a network, and the epidemic threshold. *Start:* Pastor-Satorras and Vespignani, PRL 2001.
- **SL-06 Contagion and cascades.** Threshold models, complex contagion, global cascades. *Start:* Watts, PNAS 2002. Centola and Macy, AJS 2007.
- **SL-07 Opinion dynamics.** The voter model and its relatives. *Start:* Castellano, Fortunato and Loreto, Reviews of Modern Physics 2009.
- **SL-08 Synchronization.** Coupled oscillators, and which structures synchronize easily. *Start:* Arenas et al., Physics Reports 2008.
- **SL-09 Evolutionary games.** Cooperation and defection among players arranged on a network. *Start:* Nowak and May, Nature 1992.

### Dynamics of networks

The structure itself changes.

- **SL-10 Temporal networks.** Links that appear and disappear, and paths that respect time. *Start:* Holme and Saramaki, Physics Reports 2012.
- **SL-11 Network growth.** How real networks change as they grow, and what decides where a new link goes. *Start:* Papadopoulos, Kitsak, Serrano, Boguna and Krioukov, Nature 2012. Leskovec, Kleinberg and Faloutsos, KDD 2005. Bianconi and Barabasi, EPL 2001.
- **SL-12 Adaptive networks.** Structure and node states that change each other. *Start:* Gross and Blasius, Journal of the Royal Society Interface 2008.

### Control and navigation

- **SL-13 Controllability and observability.** Which nodes to drive, and where to put the sensors. *Start:* Liu, Slotine and Barabasi, Nature 2011 and PNAS 2013.
- **SL-14 Navigability.** Finding short paths with only local information. *Start:* Kleinberg, Nature 2000.

### Structure

- **SL-15 Network motifs.** Small subgraphs that occur more often than chance allows. *Start:* Milo et al., Science 2002.
- **SL-16 Statistical models of networks.** Exponential random graph models. *Start:* Robins et al., Social Networks 2007.
- **SL-17 Core-periphery structure and node roles.** Describing position beyond group membership. *Start:* Borgatti and Everett, Social Networks 2000. Guimera and Amaral, Nature 2005.
- **SL-18 Limits of community detection.** Detectability, and the choice of the number of groups. *Start:* Decelle et al., PRL 2011.

### Machine learning on networks

- **SL-19 Link prediction.** Predicting links that are missing or yet to form, and evaluating the prediction. *Start:* Liben-Nowell and Kleinberg, JASIST 2007. Zhang and Chen, NeurIPS 2018 (SEAL).
- **SL-20 Knowledge graphs.** Networks whose links have types, and how they are embedded. *Start:* Bordes et al., NeurIPS 2013.
- **SL-21 Limits of graph neural networks.** Over-squashing, expressive power, what a per-node embedding cannot say about a pair, and explaining a prediction. *Start:* Alon and Yahav, ICLR 2021. Zhang and Chen, NeurIPS 2018 (SEAL). Ying et al., NeurIPS 2019.

### Visualization

- **SL-22 Network layout.** Force-directed placement and the alternatives. *Start:* Fruchterman and Reingold, Software: Practice and Experience 1991.
- **SL-23 Large networks on a page.** Aggregation, bundling, matrix views. *Start:* Ghoniem, Fekete and Castagliola, InfoVis 2004. Holten, IEEE TVCG 2006.

### Where the network comes from

- **SL-24 Inferring networks from data.** Correlation networks and backbone extraction. *Start:* Zalesky, Fornito and Bullmore, NeuroImage 2012. Serrano, Boguna and Vespignani, PNAS 2009.
- **SL-25 Network reconstruction.** Estimating the links when only node totals are observed, as with banks and their balance sheets. *Start:* Squartini, Caldarelli, Cimini, Gabrielli and Garlaschelli, Physics Reports 2018. Cimini et al., Nature Reviews Physics 2019.

### Networks and society

- **SL-26 Recommendation, ranking and misinformation.** What link algorithms do to groups, and how false information spreads. *Start:* Karimi et al., Scientific Reports 2018. Vosoughi, Roy and Aral, Science 2018.
